title: Russia’s Next Mobilization Is Already Happening
gist: Alexey Kovalev argues Russia does not need a new mobilization decree because it is already mobilizing by stealth: the 2022 decree was never legally ended, rising cash bonuses (~2 million rubles per contract) sustain ~1,000 sign-ups a day, and regional draft raids and pressure on conscripts fill the gap. Recruitment is strained (263,000 contracts in Jan-Sep 2026 vs 292,000 a year earlier) against 30,000-40,000 monthly casualties, but a formal call-up would only come if the quiet system visibly fails.

insights.claim: Putin's Sept. 21, 2022 decree mobilizing 300,000 men did more damage to the Kremlin's hold on Russian public opinion than anything else in nearly five years of war.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Shows open mobilization is the Kremlin's most politically costly lever, shaping how it sustains the war.

insights.claim: After the 2022 mobilization, Levada's monthly mood survey recorded its sharpest one-time collapse: Russians describing their mood as 'great' fell from 15% to 7% and those reporting fear more than tripled.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Quantifies the domestic shock a formal call-up produces, a key constraint on Kremlin escalation.

insights.claim: The share of Russians who believed the war was 'progressing successfully' fell from 73% in May 2022 to 53% by end-September 2022.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: War-confidence polling is sensitive to mobilization, a leading indicator of regime risk.

insights.claim: An estimated 300,000 to 500,000 fighting-age men left Russia within two weeks of the 2022 decree, with Kazakhstan alone recording some 400,000 arrivals from Russia by late November.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Mobilization-driven emigration drains labor and capital and boosts neighboring economies like Kazakhstan and Georgia.

insights.claim: Asking whether Russia will issue a new mobilization decree is the wrong question, because a new mobilization wave is already happening without one.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Investors waiting for a headline decree as an escalation signal may miss an ongoing force-generation process.
insights.quote: That nothing has been announced does not mean that a new mobilization wave is not happening.

insights.claim: A May 2023 Russian Supreme Court ruling holds that a mobilization period lasts until a decree formally ends it, and no such end-of-mobilization decree exists, so Russia has legally been continuously mobilized since 2022.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Legal framework lets the Kremlin expand manpower without new, market-moving announcements.
insights.quote: Legally, Russia has been continuously mobilized since 2022. Nothing requires Putin to sign anything new.

insights.claim: In July 2026 the Russian parliament expanded the pool of convicts eligible for military service under a law explicitly applying 'during mobilization, martial law, or wartime,' and an August Supreme Court ruling cited 'the period of mobilization' as an aggravating circumstance.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: The state keeps legislating on a wartime basis, signalling durable war footing.

insights.claim: The Kremlin denied mobilization plans 18 times in the three months before September's parliamentary elections, per the Moscow Times, and Putin called the rumors 'chush sobachya' and an 'information attack.'
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Official denials are an unreliable signal; in 2022 denials immediately preceded the decree.

insights.claim: Kremlin denials historically precede action: Duma Defense Committee chair Andrey Kartapolov and spokesperson Dmitry Peskov both denied plans just before the 2022 decree.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Treat Kremlin denials as weak or even inverse indicators when assessing escalation risk.
insights.quote: something isn’t true until the Kremlin denies it.
insights.locator: As Russia observers like to scoff

insights.claim: Ukraine is imposing around 30,000 to 40,000 casualties on Russian forces each month, and recruitment is strained but not breaking.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Attrition rates versus recruitment determine how long Russia can sustain current operations without escalation.

insights.claim: According to Janis Kluge's tracking of regional budget payments, about 263,000 new Russian military contracts were signed in the first nine months of 2026, down from 292,000 in the same period of 2025, with September at roughly 1,000 a day.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Declining contract signings indicate rising marginal cost of manpower and pressure toward coercion.

insights.claim: The average Russian military sign-up bonus has climbed to almost 2 million rubles (nearly $25,000) per contract, almost 30% more than last year.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Escalating bonuses add to regional and federal fiscal strain and signal a tightening labor pool.

insights.claim: In Siberia's Khanty-Mansi region the one-time military sign-up bonus is roughly 30 times the average local monthly wage.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Military pay is crowding out civilian labor markets, contributing to Russian wage pressure and labor shortages.

insights.claim: The Kremlin prefers financial inducements and ad hoc coercion to a dramatic nationwide call-up because those methods have worked so far.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Expect continued fiscal outlays on recruitment rather than a sudden mobilization shock.

insights.claim: Since June 2026 independent Russian outlets have documented draft raids in which plainclothes men in unmarked vans seize men from streets and workplaces and force them to sign contracts; legal-aid groups reported complaints from at least 17 regions by late August.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Spreading coercive recruitment signals manpower stress and rising social risk inside Russia.

insights.claim: Draft-dodger hotline Idite Lesom took three times as many calls in August 2026 as in August 2025, with targets largely indebted or legally vulnerable men in poor, remote regions.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: A tripling of help-line demand is a real-time proxy for intensifying stealth mobilization.

insights.claim: In Nizhny Tagil authorities reportedly paid private recruiters 400,000 rubles per man delivered, and a local prosecutor complained violent gangs and corrupt police joined the trade.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Bounty-based recruitment illustrates the commercialization and criminalization of Russian force generation.

insights.claim: Moscow sets regional recruitment quotas and devolves fulfillment to governors, employers and private agents, which insulates the Kremlin and Putin from association with abuses.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Decentralized coercion lowers the political cost of sustaining the war, extending its likely duration.

insights.claim: Since January 2026 Russia has run a perpetual year-round draft, with about 120,000 fall-cycle conscripts heading to units from Oct. 10, allegedly none posted to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
entities: General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces
insights.so_what: A permanent draft expands the pool from which contract soldiers can be pressured.

insights.claim: Putin's pledge not to send conscripts to fight is technically true but hollow, because conscripts are pressured into contracts that the still-active 2022 decree makes effectively indefinite.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Official force-posture pledges understate Russia's real manpower reservoir.
insights.quote: That teenage or 20-something conscripts aren’t sent to fight and die in Ukraine remains technically true while missing the point

insights.claim: Putin's past pledges have been broken: reservists were called up six months after his March 2022 pledge, and fresh conscripts were sent to repel Ukraine's August 2024 Kursk incursion.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Discount Kremlin assurances when modeling escalation scenarios.

insights.claim: Mobilization continues to fall disproportionately on poor non-ethnic-Russian and peripheral regions such as Buryatia, Dagestan, Tuva, Yakutia, Penza and Izhevsk, though draft-age men are now also being stopped in Moscow.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Spread of raids to Moscow would mark a rising political risk as costs reach the core electorate.

insights.claim: A formal new call-up is possible if the front deteriorates sharply or recruitment plummets, but it would publicly admit the quiet system failed and risk a repeat of the September 2022 shock and exodus.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: A formal decree would be a clear escalation signal with emigration, labor and sentiment shocks for Russia and neighbors.

insights.claim: United Russia won roughly 58% and 349 of 450 seats in September's parliamentary elections, its largest majority ever, with turnout secured through coercion of state employees, per Kremlin insiders speaking to Meduza.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Consolidated parliamentary control removes institutional constraints on further war measures.
